newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil aims to finish voting on reform amendments.
newsitem.headline: Brazil aims to finish voting on reform amendments.

text.p: The Brazilian government will seek to complete the time-consuming and potentially divisive process of voting on amendments to its civil service reform bill this week, congressional officials said Monday.
"If we get a really good turnout we could even finish the amendments off this week," said an aide to Deputy Benito Gama, the government's chief whip in the Chamber of Deputies.

She said telegrams were being sent to lawmakers and their travel schedules were being checked to make sure they would be in Congress in time to vote against several outstanding amendments aimed at defeating important points of the bill.
Once voting on the amendments is completed, the reform can be put to a second and final vote in the Chamber of Deputies. If approved, it advanaces to the Senate.

The bill, seen by the government as key to Brazil's attempts to reduce public spending, was approved in a first vote on the floor the lower house in April with just one vote more than the three-fifths majority of 308 needed.
In the subsequent voting on amendments, the opposition managed to strike down a central article of the bill, forcing the government to delay further voting.
The article would have allowed federal, state and municipal governments to hire workers without offering them jobs-for-life guarantees, making it easier to reduce payroll spending.
Key points of the bill which remain at risk from opposition amendments include an article allowing authorities to dimiss existing workers who enjoy job stability.
Another amendment seeks to prevent local governments from setting ceilings on pay and pensions below the 10,800 reais ($10,188) cap proposed for federal employees.

Also up for a vote is an amendment which would keep the obligatory retirement age for civil servants at 70, and not 60 as proposed in the reform, and a controversial proposal that lawmakers be exempted from the pay and pensions ceiling .

In an attempt to ensure support in the first full vote on the civil service reform bill, the government pledged its backing for that amendment and then withdrew it once the bill was initially approved in April.

Anger over the government's U-turn was seen as the major factor behind its failure last month to kill the opposition amendment ensuring job security for newly hired employees. Resentment among lawmakers may yet upset further voting.

Another complicating factor is reported to be dissatisfaction within the powerful Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) which wants President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to give it immediately two ministries currently up for grabs.
Newspapers have said Cardoso will only appoint the PMDB candidates to the Transport and Justice ministries once the civil service reform bill has cleared the Chamber of Deputies.
